Flooding is one of the most destructive natural catastrophes in the world as it yields a lot of loss of life, destruction of infrastructure, and financial disturbance. Although useful, traditional hydrological modelling techniques may be unable to cope with the complexity and non-linearity of the flood processes, especially when the climate changes. In this chapter we will explore the new and innovative methods for mapping, predicting and assessing climate impacts on flooding using Artificial Intelligence, also called AI, and Machine Learning, or ML. Additionally, we will also look into the essential ideas, data needs, models, and case studies of how AI and ML tools can be utilized for managing floods.. The case studies and examples will help the students have a glimpse of how these technologies are being utilized to improve flood risk assessment, enhance the early warning system and climate adaptation strategies.

Carbonate rock chemical weathering is a fundamental yet complex process within the global carbon cycle and constitutes an important long-term sink for atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2). During carbonate dissolution, CO2 derived from the atmosphere and/or soil is consumed and transformed into Dissolved Inorganic Carbon (DIC), predominantly in the form of bicarbonate (\begin{document}${\rm{HCO}}_3^{-}$\end{document}). This DIC is subsequently transported downstream through groundwater and surface runoff systems and may ultimately be stored in the ocean over long timescales. Because this process reduces atmospheric CO2 concentrations and, to some extent, mitigates the release of soil carbon to the atmosphere, carbonate weathering is widely regarded as an important natural mechanism for buffering anthropogenic climate warming. However, the magnitude of karst inorganic carbon sinks at the regional scale remains highly uncertain. This uncertainty is particularly pronounced in extensive karst regions, where strong spatial heterogeneity in lithological conditions, aquifer connectivity, recharge processes, and land-surface environments makes it difficult to upscale point-based hydrochemical observations to the regional level. Consequently, significant discrepancies persist in regional estimates of karst carbon sinks, and the relative contributions of climatic and environmental factors to DIC production and export have yet to be fully resolved. The Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, located in southern China, is one of the most extensive and representative karst regions in the country. It is characterized by widespread carbonate rock outcrops, well-developed epikarst and subsurface drainage systems, and hydrogeochemical processes that are highly sensitive to monsoonal climatic forcing. The region has a subtropical humid monsoon climate, abundant precipitation, and diverse geomorphological settings, all of which provide favorable conditions for carbonate weathering and dissolved carbon export. At the same time, Guangxi exhibits marked regional variability in climate, hydrology, topography, and karst development, making it an ideal study area for reassessing karst inorganic carbon sinks and exploring their controlling mechanisms at the regional scale. Against this background, the present study systematically re-evaluates the karst inorganic carbon sink in Guangxi from 2002 to 2022 and employs the Geodetector model to investigate its controlling factors.This study employs multidisciplinary methodology, integrating field observations, remote sensing data, machine learning modeling, and spatial attribution analysis. First, in consideration of the geological and hydrogeological setting of the karst region in Guangxi, a relatively large dataset of measured groundwater DIC concentrations was compiled. High-resolution remote sensing data were also selected to characterize environmental conditions relevant to karst carbon processes. Based on these multi-source datasets, machine learning models were trained and validated to reconstruct the spatiotemporal distribution of DIC concentrations in karst groundwater across Guangxi from 2002 to 2022. Compared with conventional point-based observational approaches, this method enhances the regional representativeness of the estimates and helps compensate for the limited spatial and temporal coverage of measured data. Additionally, the incorporation of remotely sensed variables provides feasible proxy indicators for certain environmental conditions that are challenging to monitor continuously over extended periods. Second, the reconstructed DIC concentration fields were combined with long-term discharge data, and the karst inorganic carbon sink generated by carbonate weathering was recalculated using the classical and widely applied hydrochemical flux method, thereby providing a more accurate representation of both temporal fluctuations and spatial variability in dissolved carbon export. Finally, the Geodetector model was employed to quantify the explanatory power of potential influencing factors through both factor detection and interaction detection, with the aim of identifying the dominant controls on the spatial differentiation of the karst carbon sink in Guangxi.The results show that: (1) From 2002 to 2022, the cumulative karst inorganic carbon sink in Guangxi reached 5.03×107 tCO2, with an annual average of 2.40 ×106 tCO2·a−1. (2) Interannual variability in the karst inorganic carbon sink was pronounced, with a marked increasing trend from 2003 to 2006, followed by an overall fluctuating upward trend thereafter. The maximum annual sink occurred in 2008, reaching 3.56×106 tCO2·a−1, whereas the minimum was recorded in 2009 at 1.44×106 tCO2·a−1, the former being approximately 2.5 times the latter. (3) The mean karst inorganic carbon sink intensity during the study period was 30.24 tCO2·km−2·a−1, with clear spatial heterogeneity. Higher values were mainly concentrated in central and northeastern Guangxi, whereas lower values occurred in the southwestern and southeastern parts of the region. (4) Geodetector analysis indicates that precipitation is the primary factor controlling the spatiotemporal variation of the karst inorganic carbon sink in Guangxi, consistent with the strong dependence of karst process on water availability. Further interaction detection reveals that the explanatory power of the interaction between any two factors is greater than that of any single factor, indicating that the formation and differentiation of the karst carbon sink exhibit significant nonlinear coupling characteristics. Among these interactions, the interaction between temperature and precipitation shows the highest explanatory power.

Groundwater is an essential source of fresh water which is used in agriculture, domestic consumption, and industries. Over-exploitation, climate changes, and population increase are reducing the level of groundwater in most areas. Proper ground water levels forecasting would be therefore critical in proper water management and sustainability. The latest researches have utilized machine and deep learning to forecast the groundwater level by making use of past hydrological and climatic records. Random Forest, Support Vector Machines, Artificial Neural Networks, and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) algorithms have demonstrated promising outcomes in ground water on capturing complex trends in groundwater datasets. Others have also combined satellite data and environmental variables to enhance the accuracy of prediction. Nonetheless, a number of current studies are area-specific, use smaller datasets, or models of individual machine learning. This complicates the situation of establishing the most effective methods of forecasting groundwater over time under comparable circumstances. In order to solve such a problem, the paper offers a machine learning-based model of improving groundwater level predictions on the basis of historical groundwater and environmental data. The approach will involve processing of data, selection of features, and applying various machine learning models to compare them. The standard evaluation metrics to be used in evaluating the performance of these models will be accuracy, RMSE, and R 2. It is hoped that, the anticipated value of this study would be identification of relevant machine learning methods to predict groundwater, and offer a systematized framework that could be used to provide a sustainable groundwater management and further research in hydrology.

Chapter 5 explores the integration of Geographic Information Systems (GIS) in surface water hydrology, emphasizing how spatial data and digital tools have transformed watershed modeling and analysis. Hydrologic models simulate the precipitation-runoff process, accounting for factors like infiltration, evaporation, soil moisture, and streamflow. GIS enables the use of high-resolution digital elevation models (DEMs), hydrographic vector data, soils, land use, climate, and precipitation datasets to more accurately represent watershed characteristics and hydrologic responses. The chapter reviews key data sources and formats, including DEMs for terrain analysis, radar and satellite imagery for precipitation estimation, and soil moisture sensors. It details GIS operations such as watershed delineation, stream network extraction, and spatial interpolation methods for rainfall data. Various hydrologic models—ranging from lumped to distributed, empirical to conceptual—are discussed, with examples like HEC-HMS, SWAT, and the National Water Model. Recent advances include the use of GeoAI and machine learning to improve flood forecasting and hydrologic predictions. The chapter highlights the challenges of model calibration and data uncertainty but underscores the growing capabilities of GIS and remote sensing in supporting robust, spatially detailed hydrologic modeling.

Freshwater brownification, characterized by the darkening of water due to increased organic carbon, has emerged as a significant environmental issue in boreal ecosystems. This dissertation investigates the primary drivers of brownification in Finnish river basins, focusing on the roles of climate change, land use changes, and forest management. Using a combination of data analysis, machine learning models, and process-based simulations, this study examines the interactions between hydrology, peatlands, and forest age structure in influencing organic carbon transport. The first study analyses long-term trends in total organic carbon (TOC) across Finnish river basins, identifying key environmental and anthropogenic factors contributing to its variations. Results indicate that brownification trends are highly variable across Finland, with a general decrease in TOC concentrations in peatland and northern river basins but an increase in southern basins. Boosted regression tree (BRT) analysis highlights forest ditching, the percentage of old forests, and wetlands as the most significant factors affecting TOC dynamics. The second study explores the effects of forest age on water quality, shifting the traditional perspective from biodiversity conservation to its role in organic carbon dynamics in the water. Findings suggest that younger forests contribute to higher TOC fluxes due to increased metabolic activity in soils, whereas older forests stabilize carbon cycles and reduce brownification. Forested headwater catchments, particularly those dominated by peatlands, exhibit the strongest link between runoff and TOC loads, reinforcing the role of land use in shaping water quality. The third study evaluates land-use strategies to mitigate brownification by integrating hydrological and biogeochemical modelling with climate change projections and forest use scenarios. Results suggest that reducing forest harvesting intensity and increasing protected forest areas can effectively limit TOC transport into freshwater systems. Additionally, climate change simulations indicate that rising temperatures and precipitation will exacerbate brownification, particularly in northern and peatland-dominated catchments. Overall, this dissertation contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of the processes driving freshwater brownification and provides policy-relevant insights for sustainable land and water management. By emphasizing the trade-offs between forestry practices and water quality, the findings support adaptive management strategies aimed at balancing carbon sequestration, biodiversity conservation, and freshwater ecosystem health in the face of a changing climate.

The increasing frequency and impact of geohazards, particularly landslides in tectonically active and climatically sensitive regions, necessitate continuous advancements in landslide and engineering geosciences.This Special Issue of the Journal of the Geological Society of India presents a collection of contributions addressing recent developments in landslide studies and engineering geosciences, with particular emphasis on the Himalayan region, China, Central Asia, and other geodynamically active terrains.It brings together a carefully curated set of papers that collectively examine contemporary challenges relating to landslide processes, hazard assessment, geotechnical behaviour, and sustainable infrastructure development.Drawing upon case studies from different parts of the world, the issue reflects both regional specificity and wider global relevance.A central focus of this issue is the application of emerging technologies to overcome the limitations associated with conventional landslide investigation methods.Several contributions demonstrate the effectiveness of high-resolution remote sensing, unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) surveys, and GIS-based modelling in capturing detailed terrain information and monitoring dynamic slope processes.These approaches significantly improve the accuracy of landslide detection, mapping, and early warning systems.Equally important is the shift towards quantitative, multi-parameter frameworks for hazard assessment.The articles adopt integrated approaches combining morphometric, morphotectonic, geotechnical, and statistical analyses to better characterise slope instability.Such frameworks provide mechanistic insights into the relationships between tectonics, geomorphology, hydrology, and anthropogenic influences, thereby enhancing predictive accuracy and supporting more effective risk zonation and mitigation strategies.Recent advances in artificial intelligence and machine learning have further Mining operations constitute one of the most significant anthropogenic contributors to global land degradation. These activities disrupt soil structure, deplete organic matter, introduce heavy metal contamination, and fundamentally alter watershed hydrology. Restoration of agricultural potential to mining-affected land demands rigorous, multi-dimensional land suitability evaluation (LSE) frameworks that transcend conventional productivity-focused land use approaches. This review critically synthesises the conceptual foundations of the FAO Framework for Land Evaluation (1976, 1983), the evolving role of soil quality indices in suitability assessment, and the contributions of GIS and remote sensing to spatial suitability mapping. Drawing on evidence from granite quarrying in semi-arid India, coal mining in eastern India and the United States, iron ore and bauxite mining in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia and gold mining in South America, the review demonstrates that standard FAO suitability classification systematically underestimates contamination risk and overestimates crop production potential in miningaffected landscapes. To address this methodological gap, a Contamination-Adjusted Suitability Index (CASI) was proposed, integrating FAO suitability scores, soil quality sub-indices and pollution load indices into a composite quantitative instrument. Recent advances in machine learning, digital soil mapping and cloud-based Earth observation are assessed for their capacity to operationalise contamination-adjusted suitability assessment at regional and global scales. High-priority research gaps are identified, including the absence of mine-type-specific FAO criteria, the underrepresentation of dimension stone quarrying in LSE literature and the disconnect between suitability science and land governance. A globally applicable integrated framework for evidence-based land rehabilitation planning is proposed.

Smart water management is a combination of artificial intelligence and advanced sensor technologies that allow optimization of the use of water resources in agricultural, urban, and environmental systems. AI-based irrigation systems use machine learning code to define soil moisture, weather condition, and crop water demand and apply this code to provide accurate water delivery to reduce consumption by 30 percent and retain crop yields. Predictive models are applied in hydrology to enable networks and remote sensing data to predict the state of water availability, risks of flooding, and droughts more accurately. The Real-time integrated monitoring organization with AI analytics such as assist in dynamic water supply, leak detection, and quality management in urban area. These smart systems contribute to the idea of sustainability of water conservation by detecting inefficiencies, automatic demand-apply. Specifically, we refer to the potentials of the integration of of AI with remote sensing, IOT-based hydrological networks, and simulation models that are designed to provide intelligent and responsive systems of water management. With the ever-growing scarcity of water in the world, the use of AI-based smart water management seems to be a vital solution to the provision of water security, agricultural sustainability, and ecosystem maintenance.

This thesis investigates the use of weather radar data for hydrological applications, specifically in rainfall estimation for flood forecasting, focusing on two major river basins in Selangor, Malaysia. Weather radar provides high-resolution rainfall estimates over large areas, addressing problems such as uneven rainfall distribution and limited rain gauge coverage. However, radar-based Quantitative Precipitation Estimation (QPE) is susceptible to errors caused by ground clutter, beam blockage, and signal attenuation. The research explores innovative techniques in radar QPE accuracy enhancement, including using artificial intelligence tools to classify rain types and improve the estimated rainfall values. Methodologies include the extraction of geometric characteristics from radar reflectivity images, including rain cell location, area, intensity, and orientation, which are then used for rainfall classification and machine learning applications. The K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) algorithm is applied to classify radar-based rainfall into convective and stratiform categories. Despite some misclassifications due to overlapping feature characteristics, the KNN model achieves strong predictive performance with an Area Under the Curve (AUC) greater than 90%. In addition, an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) model is designed using the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm and rain gauge data to improve the accuracy of radar-based QPE. The performance of the ANN-enhanced QPE model is evaluated using Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) and correlation metrics, showing a significant reduction in RMSE from 11.40 mm/h to 4.76 mm/h, thus enhancing the precision of radar-based rainfall estimates. The improved radar QPE model is then applied as input to an integrated flood forecasting system, employing the HEC-HMS hydrological model, with a novelty of merging process of the gridded-based QPE as sub-basin rainfall. The integrated system is applied for flood simulation in the Klang and Langat River Basins, with calibration results demonstrating that rain gauge data and ANN-calibrated QPE produces the highest correlation followed by uncalibrated radar QPE. The integration of calibrated radar QPE with hydrological models presents a promising approach for improving flood forecasting and predicting extreme weather events such as flash floods. This research contributes to advancements in radar hydrology, hybrid machine learning techniques for feature extraction, enhanced rainfall estimation methods, and improved radar-based rainfall-runoff models for better flood forecasting and warning systems in river basins in Malaysia.

Landslides are among the most frequent and destructive geological hazards in Indonesia, particularly in mountainous regions with steep slopes, complex geomorphology, and high rainfall.In addition to their role as natural hazards, landslides act as significant drivers of environmental disturbance and land degradation, highlighting the need for reliable susceptibility assessment as part of environmental monitoring and sustainable land-use planning.This study applies a random forest (RF) machine learning model integrated with geographic information systems (GIS) to support environmental monitoring of landslide-prone landscapes in the Tinggimoncong District, Gowa Regency, South Sulawesi, Indonesia.A balanced dataset of 440 sample points (220 landslide and 220 non-landslide locations) was constructed using high-resolution imagery, field verification, and official records, and combined with twelve conditioning factors representing topography, geology, hydrology, land cover, and human activities.Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, F1-score, ROC-AUC, and PR-AUC.The RF model demonstrated high predictive performance (AUC = 0.971; F1-score = 0.95).Feature importance analysis indicates that slope aspect, elevation, slope gradient, and distance to roads are the dominant factors controlling environmentally driven slope instability.The resulting probabilistic and classified susceptibility maps identify zones of high environmental instability that spatially correspond with areas prone to land degradation due to recurrent landslides.The proposed RF-based framework provides a robust basis for environmental monitoring, land degradation management, and sustainable spatial planning in complex tropical terrains.

Abstract. From typhoon rainfall to slope failure, this study addresses the urgent need for typhoon-adapted hazard warning systems in mountainous regions like Zixing City, China. We develop an integrated framework to optimize dynamic susceptibility models and rainfall thresholds by leveraging machine learning and spatiotemporal rainfall analysis. Using buffer-based negative sampling (0.1–5.0 km) and variable weighting methods (IV, CF, FR), we compare SVM and LightGBM models. The SVM model with FR input at 0.5 km buffer achieved the highest accuracy (AUC=0.913), correctly classifying 86.4 % of landslides in high-risk zones, revealing how typhoon-driven hydrology interacts with slope instability. For rainfall thresholds, the H24-D7 model (24-hour intensity vs. 7-day antecedent rainfall) emerged as optimal (71.8 % accuracy), effectively capturing typhoon-specific triggers like short-term downpours and cumulative soil saturation. Kriging interpolation generated spatially explicit thresholds, identifying granite slopes and road-proximal areas as hotspots for typhoon-induced failures. The final hazard warning system, integrating susceptibility and dynamic thresholds, showed 71.4 % overlap with historical landslides, emphasizing the critical role of typhoon rainfall dynamics in slope failure prediction. This work provides a scalable approach for regions facing typhoon-related landslide risks, prioritizing both spatial heterogeneity and temporal rainfall patterns.

Artificial neural networks, and in particular multilayer perceptrons and recurrent networks, have gained an immense popularity in recent years as data-driven modelling tools in hydraulics and hydrology since they can be made to perform reasonably well in most cases of practical interest. However, there are also some legitimate concerns on some aspects of ANNs which may still need further investigation. For instance, the network’s architecture has to be determined a priori or modified while training by some heuristic which may not necessarily result in an optimal structure of the network ( Smola, 1996 ). A large number of inputs to a network usually results in a more complicated architecture with a greater number of parameters to be optimized. Moreover, the capacity of the networks is controlled only indirectly by such methods as stopping the training early, pruning or weight decay in order to obtain better generalisation. Neural networks can sometimes get stuck in local minima while training, making the network unable to approximate the data set. There are a number of researches directed towards addressing these problems and some have resulted in a more general form of learning systems, called Support Vector Machines (SVMs).

Mining is inherently spatial, requiring detailed knowledge of geology, topography, hydrology, and infrastructure for informed decision-making across the lifecycle. Geographic Information Systems (GIS) have become essential for managing spatial complexity, integrating multidimensional datasets, and supporting predictive analytics in mining engineering and management. This review adopts a structured approach to synthesize current knowledge on GIS applications across the mining lifecycle, drawing from peer-reviewed journals, conference proceedings, and technical reports published between 2000 and 2025. Literature was systematically analyzed and categorized according to exploration, mine planning, operation and production, environmental monitoring, and post-mining land use. In exploration, GIS facilitates mineral potential mapping by integrating geological, geophysical, and geochemical data with remote sensing imagery, using multi-criteria decision analysis and fuzzy logic to handle uncertainty. During mine planning, GIS supports site selection, pit design, infrastructure layout, and resource estimation, often linked with 3D modeling and specialized mine planning software. In operations, GIS dashboards combined with IoT and SCADA systems enable real-time monitoring of equipment, personnel, and environmental conditions, enhancing production efficiency and safety. GIS also underpins environmental monitoring and post-mining rehabilitation through pollution mapping, tailings dam assessment, land-use suitability analysis, and time-series remote sensing. Despite its versatility, GIS adoption faces challenges, including data availability, integration complexity, computational demands, and skill gaps. Emerging technologies such as AI, machine learning, IoT, cloud-based platforms, and Augmented Reality and Virtual Reality (AR/VR) offer opportunities to overcome these limitations and advance smart, sustainable mining. This review highlights GIS as a transformative tool for optimizing operations, mitigating risks, and supporting environmental stewardship, emphasizing the need for continued innovation, interdisciplinary collaboration, and standardized workflows to fully realize its potential.

Soil salinity is a significant cause of soil issues in dry and semi-dry regions. It can occur naturally or as a result of human activity. Increased soil salinity adversely affects agricultural productivity, ultimately resulting in land degradation. Soil salinization significantly affects agriculture, economics, hydrology, geochemistry, climate, and soil ecology. Regular and precise monitoring and mapping of soil salinity is crucial for soil reclamation, which aims to reduce or prevent further increases in soil salt levels. Remote sensing has supplanted conventional methods in evaluating soil salinity by offering expedited, more precise, and more advanced approaches for mapping and monitoring soil salinity. The main objective of this study is to use remote sensing data, geographic information systems, and machine learning algorithms to draw a soil salinity map for Diyala Governorate in 2024. During the field survey of the study area, 70 soil models were collected in the period from 19 to 26 January 2024, synchronized with Sentinel1 and Sentinel-2 images. The data was trained using three machine learning algorithms: "artificial neural network (ANN), support vector machine (SVM), and random forest (RF)". The RF model outperformed ANN and SVM with the RMSE= 0.48 ds.m⁻¹, and MAE= 0.23 ds.m⁻¹. Results indicated that by combining Various remote sensing sensors data and field data and utilizing a suitable machine learning model, it is possible to generate accurate salinity maps for monitoring soil salinity as an environmental issue.

Soil salinization is a significant environmental and agricultural issue, particularly in semi-arid and arid regions. The salinization could be voluntary or human-caused. Excessive salinity in the soil has a detrimental effect on the production and expansion of agriculture, ultimately resulting in land degradation. This complex, dynamic process significantly affects agriculture, the economy, hydrology, geochemistry, climate, and the soil environment. Early monitoring and mapping of salinity are essential for the effective execution of soil reclamation initiatives that aim to reduce or prevent future increases in soil salinity. Remote sensing (RS) provides faster, more accurate, and more skilled means of mapping and tracking salinity; it has supplanted older approaches for this resolution. This study aims to review the literature and establish a connection between remote sensing (RS), geographic information systems (GIS), and machine learning (ML). To achieve this objective, a total of 10 papers from both foreign and local sources were studied for a period spanning from 2017 to 2023. The authors extensively utilized the Landsat and Sentinel data sets, employing spectral indicators such as NDVI and SI to assess soil salinity. Furthermore, supervised machine learning methods, such as Random Forest (RF), support vector machine (SVM), and Extreme Gradient Boost (XGBoost), have gained increased popularity in their applications. This integration has significant potential for enhancing the precision of prediction and analysis models in generating maps and analyzing spatial data. Recent research has found that this integration tends to reduce the likelihood of agricultural land loss due to salinity.

Significance Rainfall-induced clustered landslides are among the most destructive regional geohazards in the mountainous areas of southeastern China. The region is characterized by intense tectonic fragmentation, deeply weathered granite, tuff, and sandstone–mudstone formations, widespread residual-colluvial deposits, low-mountain and hilly terrain, dense vegetation, and extensive engineering activities. These conditions create highly heterogeneous slope structures and provide a favorable geological setting for the simultaneous or successive failure of numerous slopes during extreme rainfall. Under typhoon rainstorms, prolonged Meiyu rainfall, and short-duration intense precipitation, rainfall infiltration, surface runoff, subsurface flow, and perched groundwater may act together to weaken soil and rock masses, increase pore-water pressure, and rapidly reduce slope stability. Clustered landslides therefore commonly exhibit multiple initiation sites, abrupt occurrence, broad spatial distribution, complex motion, and rapid transformation from sliding to flowing. Recent events in Taishun, Zhejiang Province, and Wuping, Fujian Province, demonstrate that thousands of landslides can be triggered within a single rainfall episode, producing severe casualties, infrastructure disruption, and economic losses. Accurate risk identification and prevention of such hazards are essential for safeguarding mountain settlements, transportation corridors, and critical infrastructure, and for promoting a transition from post-disaster response and isolated slope treatment to proactive, regional, and system-oriented risk governance.Progress Considerable progress has been made in understanding the initiation and evolution of rainfall-induced landslides. Existing studies have clarified that intense rainfall is the direct external trigger, whereas the development of weathering profiles, the thickness and heterogeneity of residual-colluvial deposits, the morphology of bedrock interfaces, and the spatial distribution of fractures and groundwater constitute important internal controls. Rainfall infiltration and runoff alter the hydrological state of slopes, promote the formation of shallow perched water, increase pore-water pressure, and reduce effective stress and shear strength. Field investigations, laboratory tests, physical model experiments, and numerical simulations have been used to examine slope initiation, sliding, material transport, and deposition. However, most studies have focused on individual slopes or single geological units. The regional transition from local instability to concentrated slope failures remains insufficiently understood, particularly when geological structure, weathering characteristics, rainfall variability, topography, vegetation, and human disturbance interact across multiple spatial and temporal scales. Progress has also been achieved in hazard identification, monitoring, and early warning. Empirical rainfall intensity–duration thresholds based on historical events remain useful for regional warning. Geological structure, lithology, terrain parameters, land use, and susceptibility information have increasingly been integrated with rainfall data to improve spatial identification. Optical remote sensing, time-series interferometric synthetic aperture radar, airborne light detection and ranging, unmanned aerial vehicles, and ground-based monitoring provide observations of surface morphology, deformation, rainfall, soil moisture, and pore-water pressure. Statistical, physically based, and data-driven approaches, including machine learning, have been developed to integrate multi-source information. Nevertheless, existing systems are still more effective for known hazards and slowly deforming landslides than for abrupt clustered landslides with weak or non-significant precursory deformation. Dense vegetation, cloud cover, radar decorrelation, limited ground coverage, inconsistent temporal and spatial resolutions, and insufficient sharing of heterogeneous datasets continue to constrain reliable identification and short-term warning. Regional rainfall warning and site-specific deformation monitoring also remain weakly connected. Regional landslide risk assessment has gradually expanded from susceptibility and hazard zoning to frameworks that incorporate hazard, exposure, vulnerability, and potential losses. Probability analysis, scenario simulation, machine learning, high-resolution terrain data, remote sensing, and socioeconomic information have improved the spatial detail of risk representation. Risk prevention has correspondingly shifted from single-slope engineering toward graded regional management and the coordinated use of drainage, structural reinforcement, ecological restoration, monitoring, warning, emergency response, and spatial planning. Even so, many existing assessments remain static and depend heavily on historical inventories. They do not adequately represent the time-varying effects of rainfall sequences, changing slope conditions, cascading impacts, and accumulated risk under repeated or prolonged rainfall. Regional differences in settlement distribution, infrastructure connectivity, engineering conditions, and disaster-response capacity are also insufficiently reflected. As a result, current methods cannot fully support both short-term emergency decisions and medium- to long-term resilience planning. To address these limitations, a research framework organized around mechanism cognition, identification and early warning, and risk prevention and control is proposed. The first research component focuses on the multi-factor and multi-scale initiation mechanisms and dynamic evolution of clustered landslides. Historical disaster records, field surveys, drilling, geophysical exploration, multi-source remote sensing, laboratory testing, physical modeling, and numerical simulation are combined to identify dominant controlling factors, characterize spatial differences in susceptible geological structures, and clarify the coupled effects of geology, hydrology, ecology, topography, rainfall, and engineering disturbance. The evolution from stable conditions to critical failure, multiple initiation, flow transformation, convergence, and regional expansion is examined to establish a process-based understanding of clustered landslides. The second component focuses on multi-source hazard identification and short-term early warning. Airborne light detection and ranging, optical imagery, interferometric synthetic aperture radar, rainfall observations, geological-environmental data, and ground monitoring are integrated to extract microtopographic, deformation, surface-cover, hydrological, and meteorological features. A hazard-identification indicator system is developed for densely vegetated areas and for landslides lacking clear deformation precursors. Mechanism-constrained models and data-driven algorithms are combined to support rapid regional screening, refined identification of key areas, graded warning for critical slopes and high-risk zones, and dynamic updating during rainfall events. Historical-event replay and observations from representative areas are used for model calibration and validation. The third component focuses on dynamic risk assessment and collaborative resilience-based defense. Uncertainty in geological conditions, rainfall input, slope response, and exposed elements is quantified through statistical, probabilistic, numerical, and machine-learning methods. Dynamic risk models are established by coupling hazard, exposure, vulnerability, and loss consequences across multiple time scales. Risk evolution is evaluated from event response to medium- and long-term trends. Resilience indicators are developed for mountain settlements, transportation corridors, and infrastructure systems from the perspectives of resistance, emergency response, and recovery. Engineering measures such as slope reinforcement, drainage, protective barriers, and ecological restoration are coordinated with non-engineering measures including monitoring, warning, risk zoning, emergency evacuation, and management control to form a regional collaborative defense strategy.Conclusions and Prospects Rainfall-induced clustered landslides in southeastern China are governed by strong spatial heterogeneity and complex coupling among geological, hydrological, meteorological, ecological, and anthropogenic factors. Their prevention requires an integrated understanding of initiation, dynamic evolution, hazard identification, short-term warning, risk accumulation, and system resilience. Future research should connect rock–soil, individual-slope, slope-group, watershed, settlement, and regional scales; improve observation of abrupt hazards without significant deformation precursors; strengthen the integration of physical mechanisms with artificial intelligence; and establish dynamic risk maps and warning products that can be updated during rainfall. The proposed framework is expected to reveal the initiation–triggering–evolution mechanisms of clustered landslides, establish a multi-source intelligent identification and short-term warning system, develop multi-time-scale dynamic risk assessment methods, and form a regional collaborative resilience-based defense system. These advances will support disaster-prevention planning, monitoring and warning networks, engineering mitigation, territorial spatial management, and resilience enhancement in mountainous communities of southeastern China.

Wind-driven erosion, transport and redistribution of snow has strong impact on the spatial variability of snow accumulation in mountain terrain and polar regions and therefore plays an important role in the mass balance of mountain glaciers and polar ice bodies as well as in alpine hydrology. With the small-scale nature of wind systems in mountain terrain and the associated snow redistribution, modeling approaches are in the fundamental conflict between representing the non-linear atmosphere-snow interaction at relevant scales on the one hand and feasible computation demand for long-term applications on the other hand. As a result, drifting snow studies in mountain terrain either relied on highly simplified representations of the atmosphere, or were restricted to short case studies. Apart form that, drifting snow is typically not included as a process in state-of-the-art glacier mass balance models. To address this gap, this thesis aims to build a framework to model the wind-driven transport of snow, especially in mountain environments. For this, two models have been developed within this thesis: a drifting snow module included in a numerical weather model, and a machine-learning (ML) based emulator model, trained with data from the numerical model. The drifting snow module is implemented in the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model. In a first publication, the module is introduced and tested in an idealized environment and in a second article the module is applied to a short case study on Hintereisferner, a glacier in the Austrian Alps. The drifting snow module is directly coupled to the numerical model and executed with every integration time step of WRF. Snow is eroded from the ground, depending on snow density and surface shear stress and transported by the resolved wind and turbulent diffusion with a superimposed subsidence. Additionally, sublimation from drifting snow particles can be calculated, together with the associated cooling and moistening effect on the surrounding atmosphere. Sensitivity experiments showed physical consistency and mass conservation in the model. Apart from that, the results showed that the sublimation feedback locally dampens subsequent sublimation, as well as having a non-local effect on the downstream temperature, moisture and wind field structure. This shows the importance of a direct coupling between the atmospheric model and the drifting snow module, in order to account for this feedback effect. The real-world application study focuses on a drifting snow event spanning 24 h. The event is characterized by a first phase of fresh snow fall, followed by ceasing snow falls and increased winds, leading to substantial amounts of snow redistribution. Three terrestrial laser scans before and after the event, and after the phase of snow fall could be used to quantify the amounts of snow accumulation and redistribution. Additionally, Large-Eddy simulations (LES) with WRF and the drifting snow module were conducted at a horizontal resolution of Δx = 48 m. Validation of the LES with data from three automated weather stations showed a good representation of the local flow field in the simulations. Comparison of the simulated snow redistribution to the observed snow height change showed a good overall agreement at slope-scale patterns like the placement and strength of erosion zones around ridges. The third paper introduces the ML emulator model SNOWstorm as a computationally efficient downscaling tool for near-surface wind and redistribution, capable of representing non-linear atmosphere-snow interaction at low enough computation cost for multi-seasonal applications. The model is designed to predict high-resolution fields of near-surface winds, rates of snow mass change on the ground due to erosion and deposition, the vertically integrated sublimation rate, as well as the vertically integrated snow transport rate with coarse-resolution meteorological input and high-resolution terrain information. In order to have the model applicable for winter-time settings in mid- to high latitude mountain environments, the model is trained on data, reflecting the variability found in these environments. For this, a total of 720 simulations are run with WRF and the coupled drifting snow module at horizontal resolutions of Δx = 50 m over different synthetic topographies and with atmospheric conditions, representing the variability found in winter-time mountain environments of mid- to high latitudes. The stabilized steady-state fields of near-surface winds, and snow redistribution and sublimation are used as target values for the ML model to learn from the coarse-scale atmospheric input. Crossvalidation experiments showed reasonable performance of SNOWstorm simulating flow patterns and redistribution. The case study of the second article was re-visited as a first real-world application study of SNOWstorm. Validation of SNOWstorm predictions with the LES and observations shows an overall agreement of the flow patterns predicted by SNOWstorm, like the acceleration and flow deflection in ridge and summit regions, while minor discrepancies are still present. The overall patterns of snow redistribution agree between SNOWstorm predictions and the LES. Differences, like an underestimation of maximum snow erosion in summit regions by SNOWstorm is consistent with differences in the predicted flow field. Compared to the highly resolved numerical simulations of the LES, the predictions of SNOWstorm are about five orders of magnitude computationally less expensive. Overall, the two new models build a framework for future investigations on drifting snow. With the inclusion in a physics-based numerical model the drifting snow module in WRF can be used in more studies focusing on process understanding in the snow-atmosphere interaction in mountain environments as well as in polar regions. The computationally efficient calculations of SNOWstorm open the door for multi-seasonal assessments on the importance of drifting snow on glacier mass balance under different climatic and topographic settings.

Restricted-access data and code record for the manuscript "Can machine learning predict glacier mass balance for hydrology in unmonitored mountain ranges? A leave-one-region-out test against temperature-index modelling on 184 glaciers using climate reanalysis" (Swati Tak; submitted to Journal of Hydrology). Contents: frozen study protocol with SHA-256 freeze record and deviation log; Python 2.7/NumPy code (data retrieval, feature construction, climatology, temperature-index, ridge, random forest, gradient boosting and neural-network models, leave-one-glacier-out and leave-one-region-out cross-validation, statistics, figures, manuscript builder); MERRA-2 daily climate series (NASA POWER) for each WGMS glacier; glacier-year table, cross-validated predictions and result tables; ArcGIS 10.8 map documents and shapefiles (glacier sample, study regions, RGI 6.2 outlines of sample glaciers); figures. Files are available from the author on reasonable request.

Increasing heavy rainfall associated with climate change and the continued advance of urbanization have heightened the importance of spatially identifying flood-prone areas and responding proactively. This study constructed a nationwide 100 m grid flood susceptibility map and compared the spatial generalization performance of CatBoost, XGBoost, and a patch-based CNN under the same input data and spatial partitioning. Flood labels were constructed from 38,003 flood-trace polygons collected through the National Disaster and Safety Portal API. Eleven spatial variables related to topography, hydrology, land cover, vegetation, soil, and geology were used as inputs following quality inspection, correction, and reconstruction. Busan Metropolitan City was excluded entirely from training, early stopping, and model selection, and its 65,727 valid grid cells (natural flood rate, 3.50%) were used as a geographic external evaluation set. In non-Busan areas, 16 km spatial blocks and a 1.6 km buffer were applied to prevent spatial overlap between training and evaluation patches. In the Busan external evaluation, the ROC-AUC values of the three models were similar, ranging from 0.831 to 0.835, whereas the CNN achieved the highest PR-AUC (0.142) and F1-score (0.204)—4.1 times the random-prediction baseline, compared with 2.7 and 2.8 for CatBoost and XGBoost—indicating a reduction in false positives while comparable recall was maintained. The relative advantage of the models varied by evaluation metric, indicating the need to interpret ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, and fixed-threshold metrics together under conditions of natural class imbalance and when evaluating on a city unseen during training.
Data and code for the WRR submission: "When Good Predictions Get the Hydrology Wrong: Comparing Input Attributions in Hydrologic and Machine-Learning Models"

These are hydrometeorological datasets obtained from US national data repositories as inputs to a hydrologic model and model simulations over the St. Joseph River Watershed (SJRW) for both gauged and hypothetical ungauged scenarios. The datasets purpose is to demonstrate the applicability of the machine learning-based Limits of Acceptability (LoA) method and hydrologic signatures to evaluate the Sacramento Soil Moisture Accounting (SAC-SMA). This dataset is associated with the following publication: Gupta, A., M.M. Hantush, and R.S. Govindaraju. Evaluation of hydrological models at gauged and ungauged basins using machine learning-based limits-of-acceptability and hydrological signatures. JOURNAL OF HYDROLOGY. Elsevier Science Ltd, New York, NY, USA, 641: 131774, (2024).

Abstract. Land surface model (LSM) parameters translate vegetation, soil, snow, and hydrological properties into process controls on water, energy, and carbon exchange. Many of these parameters are not directly measurable at the grid scale, and their effective values depend on model structure, spatial aggregation, and observational constraints. Here we present the Adaptive Differentiable Ecohydrological Land Model (ADELM) v1.0, a fully differentiable LSM that combines process-based equations with machine learning, allowing each parameter to be prescribed or learned from observations and making parameterization itself a learnable and diagnosable part of the land model. ADELM couples canopy radiative transfer, soil hydraulics, photosynthesis, evapotranspiration, and snow and soil hydrology within a single automatic-differentiation graph, so that selected parameters can be learned directly from observed fluxes or states. Because a learned parameter can be expressed as a function of gridded environmental attributes, mappings trained at sparse sites can be applied across continuous spatial domains. We demonstrate ADELM in a European application using evapotranspiration and gross primary productivity constraints from eddy covariance sites. Mappings learned at the sites are evaluated across the 0.1° European grid, where observation-constrained learning improves evapotranspiration simulation and produces spatially coherent flux and parameter fields. Greater parameter flexibility can leave the learned parameters less identifiable, so learned parameterizations need to be judged by the stability and coherence of their parameter fields. Overall, ADELM provides a differentiable foundation for developing parameterizations that can be learned from observations, applied across space, and diagnosed for reliability.

In recent years, machine learning (ML) has witnessed growing prominence and popularity in hydrological science, offering convenience and ease of use without requiring extensive hydrological expertise or the complexity associated with process-based models.There exists debate regarding optimal training approaches, with some researchers advocating for multibasin training while questioning the validity of single-basin approaches.This study examines the relationship between training dataset size (number of basins) and model performance.Through comparative analysis, we found that increasing the number of basins for ML training does not necessarily guarantee improved performance of the trained ML model.Specifically, the state-of-the-art global ML (G model) trained by Google with nearly 6,000 global basins underperforms compared to regional ML models trained with hundreds of basins in contiguous US and Great Britain regions for predicting streamflow in both gauged and ungauged basins.Furthermore, we compared the G model with our single-basin (S) ML models, trained for 609 global locations individually, and found that the G model does not consistently outperform S models, as results show S models outperforming the G model in 46% of case studies.Therefore, the training approach should not be a criterion for judging model validity; instead, the focus should be on the trained model's performance. IntroductionWith the rapid advancement of science and technology, applications of Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) in hydrology have become increasingly popular (Ng et al., 2023; Tripathy and Mishra, 2023).Since 2018, there has been a significant surge in research publications related to ML-based streamflow forecasting, especially using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, with multiple studies published annually demonstrating the substantial potential of novel ML architectures (Shen, 2018).Numerous studies have shown that ML can often provide higher accuracy of streamflow simulations than traditional hydrological models (Kratzert et al.
